17597: Jesus announces the kingdom of God
17601: Mark summarises Jesus' preaching as the announcement that the appointed time has arrived and God's kingdom has drawn near, with a call to repent and believe the good news. In the Nazareth synagogue Luke has him read Isaiah 61 and claim its fulfilment: good news for the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind. Healings, exorcisms and table fellowship with sinners are presented as signs that God's reign is breaking in, and Jesus also warns of judgment and Gehenna.
17605: Jesus teaches about the kingdom mostly in parables: seed growing secretly, the mustard seed, hidden treasure, the pearl, the wheat and weeds, the lost sheep, coin and son. The parables picture God's reign as small and hidden now but certain to grow, as a gift of searching grace to the lost, and as ending in a final sorting and judgment. How much of the kingdom is present versus future in these parables is one of the central debates in Gospels scholarship.
17610: Peter reads the outpouring of the Spirit as Joel's last-days promise fulfilled. His sermon centres on Jesus' resurrection and exaltation: the one Israel crucified God has raised and made both Lord and Messiah. He calls hearers to repent and be baptised in Jesus' name for forgiveness of sins and promises the gift of the Spirit. Heaven and hell as individual destinations are not mentioned; the frame is Israel's story reaching its climax.
17612: Peter in Solomon's Portico: times of refreshing
17615: After a healing at the temple gate Peter again proclaims the crucified and raised Jesus as the servant of the God of Abraham. He calls for repentance so that sins may be wiped out and times of refreshing may come, and says heaven must hold Jesus until the time for restoring all things spoken by the prophets (Acts 3:21). This is the clearest Acts text joining personal repentance to a cosmic restoration hope and the return of Christ.
17620: Stephen retells Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon, stressing that God was never confined to the land or the temple and that Israel repeatedly resisted God's messengers. He sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. His death triggers persecution that scatters believers beyond Jerusalem.
17621: The message moves outward from the temple and Judea; the scattering leads to preaching in Samaria and Antioch, and the witness Saul later becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.
17623: Paul in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
17626: Paul's longest synagogue sermon in Acts runs Israel's story from the exodus to David and presents Jesus as David's promised descendant, raised from the dead. Through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and everyone who believes is set free from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. When many Jews reject this, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles.
17629: Thessalonica: turning to God and waiting for his Son
17633: Paul's earliest surviving letter recalls what his preaching produced: Gentiles turning from idols to serve the living God and to wait for his Son from heaven, who rescues from the coming wrath. Acts says he argued from the scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and opponents accused the missionaries of proclaiming another king, Jesus. Expectation of an imminent return is strong here.
17636: To a Gentile, philosophically trained audience Paul begins with creation rather than Israel's scriptures: the one God made the world, does not live in shrines, and is near to all. He calls for repentance because God has fixed a day to judge the world through a man he appointed, and has given proof by raising him from the dead. Mention of resurrection divides the hearers.
17639: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the gospel he passed on as of first importance: Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses. Most scholars regard this as a pre-Pauline formula dating within a few years of the crucifixion. He then expands it into the reign of Christ until every enemy, death last of all, is defeated and God is all in all.
17642: Romans: righteousness revealed, faith and Lordship
17645: Romans opens by defining the gospel as concerning God's Son, descended from David and declared Son of God in power by resurrection, aimed at the obedience of faith among the nations. It then argues that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin, and that God's righteousness is revealed through the faithfulness of or faith in Jesus, apart from works of the law. Confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised him leads to salvation, and the whole creation waits for liberation.
17648: The Didache: the two ways and watchfulness
17651: This church manual opens with the way of life and the way of death, a moral catechesis drawing on the Sermon on the Mount, before baptism. Its eucharistic prayers give thanks for life, knowledge and immortality made known through Jesus and pray for the scattered church to be gathered into God's kingdom. It closes with a call to watch, because the Lord will come and the world-deceiver will appear first.
17654: 1 Clement: repentance, resurrection and justification by faith
17655: Writing to settle a dispute at Corinth, the Roman church holds up Peter and Paul as noble examples who suffered unto death. It urges repentance, which God has offered in every generation, and argues for a future resurrection from nature's cycles and the phoenix. It states that believers are justified not through their own wisdom or piety but through faith, while also urging humble good works and order.
17657: Ignatius of Antioch: the real flesh of Christ
17658: Smyrna and Troas (letters on the road to Rome)
17659: Under guard on the way to martyrdom, Ignatius insists against docetists that Jesus was truly born, truly suffered and truly rose in the flesh. Salvation is union with this Christ through the eucharist, which he calls the medicine of immortality, and unity with the bishop. The gospel is cast as life and incorruption overcoming death rather than primarily as legal acquittal.
17663: Polycarp of Smyrna: grace, resurrection, judgment
17665: Polycarp's letter to the Philippians echoes Ephesians: believers are saved by grace, not by works, through the will of God in Jesus Christ. It joins this to the resurrection, the coming judgment of the living and the dead, and a call to righteous living. The later account of his martyrdom presents faithful confession of Christ as King over against swearing by Caesar's fortune.
17666: The Shepherd of Hermas: a second repentance
17668: This visionary book was widely read and sometimes treated as scripture. Its central message is a call to repentance addressed to baptised Christians who have sinned, offering one further opportunity for repentance before the building of the church (the tower) is finished. Moral purity, simplicity and care for the poor dominate its preaching.
17669: The question of what happens when the baptised sin seriously moves to the centre of pastoral preaching. Many historians see Hermas as an early step toward a formal system of post-baptismal penance; others stress that its offer is pastoral and eschatological rather than institutional.
17671: Justin Martyr: the Logos, baptism and the coming kingdom
17672: Justin presents Christianity to the emperor as the true philosophy: the divine Logos, partially sown in all people, became fully incarnate in Jesus. He describes baptism as illumination and rebirth, and the Sunday gathering of readings, prayer, eucharist and collection for the poor. He warns of eternal punishment by fire and, in his Dialogue, expects a thousand-year reign in a rebuilt Jerusalem, while noting that some orthodox Christians thought otherwise.
17679: A prophetic movement claimed fresh revelation from the Paraclete, called for stricter discipline (fasting, restrictions on remarriage, no flight from persecution) and expected the heavenly Jerusalem to descend in Phrygia. It combined Spirit, urgency and rigour, and later won Tertullian's sympathy.
17680: The wider church's rejection of the movement strengthened episcopal authority and caution about new prophecy and date-setting. Historians debate how far the movement's reputation reflects hostile sources.
17681: Irenaeus: recapitulation and the restored creation
17683: Against gnostic teachers who despised matter, Irenaeus summarised the apostolic rule of faith: one God the Creator, one Christ incarnate, crucified, raised and coming again, and the Spirit who spoke through the prophets. Christ recapitulates humanity, retracing Adam's path obediently and so undoing disobedience and death. Salvation includes the bodily resurrection and a renewed earth, with a literal earthly kingdom for the righteous before the final new creation.
17685: Tertullian: rule of faith, penance, satisfaction
17687: Tertullian defends the rule of faith against heretics and coins Latin vocabulary (trinitas, persona) for later theology. On repentance he describes exomologesis, a public discipline of confession, fasting and humiliation for serious sins after baptism, and uses the language of making satisfaction to God. He also writes vividly of the coming judgment and the punishment of persecutors, and in later life embraced the New Prophecy's rigour.
17688: Western preaching acquires a legal and penitential vocabulary (merit, satisfaction, debt) that later medieval penance and, in a different way, Anselm would develop. Whether this was a distortion or a natural Latin idiom is disputed.
17691: Clement of Alexandria: the Logos as teacher and new song
17692: Clement's *Exhortation to the Greeks* invites pagans to leave the myths and mysteries for the Logos, the new song who tunes humanity to God. Salvation is pictured as education and ascent: the Word became human so that humans might learn how to become godlike. Punishment after death is treated as largely corrective, and the true gnostic is the mature Christian who grows in love and knowledge.
17694: Origen: rule of faith, ascent and restoration
17696: Origen opens *On First Principles* by listing what the apostles plainly taught (one God, Christ, the Spirit, free will, resurrection, judgment) and then explores open questions. He speculates that God's discipline aims at healing and that the end will be like the beginning, with God all in all, possibly including the restoration of all rational beings. He was also a prolific preacher whose homilies centre on spiritual progress and moral transformation through the scriptures.
17699: Constantine and the Edict of Milan
17703: Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant Christians and all others freedom of worship and to restore confiscated church property. Constantine, who attributed his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the Christian God, began to patronise the church with buildings, privileges and imperial attention to its disputes.
17704: The church moved from persecuted minority to favoured institution. Preaching now addressed mass audiences, many only partly committed; catechesis lengthened and baptism was often delayed. Some historians see a loss of the kingdom's countercultural edge ('Constantinianism', a critique associated with Anabaptist and later writers such as John Howard Yoder); others, such as Peter Leithart, argue this is overstated.
17707: Athanasius explains why the Word became flesh: humanity, made in God's image, was sliding back into corruption and death, and only the Creator Word could renew it. By taking a mortal body and offering it in death on behalf of all, he paid the debt of death and destroyed its power, and by rising he gave incorruption. The famous summary is that he became human so that we might be made divine. The work is dated c. 318 by some and c. 335–337 by others.
17713: Bishops called by Constantine rejected Arius' view that the Son was a created being and confessed the Son as of the same essence (homoousios) as the Father. The creed says he came down for us and for our salvation, became incarnate, suffered, rose, ascended and will come to judge the living and the dead.
17714: The gospel's identity question (who is Jesus?) is fixed in creedal, philosophical language and enforced with imperial backing. The creed later expanded at Constantinople (381) to add the Spirit, one baptism for forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Critics argue the creeds skip from birth to death and say nothing of Jesus' kingdom preaching; defenders reply they were never meant as a full gospel summary.
17715: The Cappadocians: healing what is assumed
17719: The Cappadocians defended the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit, shaping the creed of Constantinople (381). Gregory of Nazianzus argued that what Christ did not assume he did not heal, so the incarnation must be complete. Gregory of Nyssa's *Catechetical Oration*, a handbook for teaching converts, explains the cross partly through the image of the devil deceived by the hidden divinity (like a fish taking bait) and looks toward a final healing in which even the originator of evil is cured; Nazianzen, by contrast, questioned ransom-to-the-devil language.
17721: John Chrysostom: the preacher of repentance and almsgiving
17723: Chrysostom preached verse-by-verse through Matthew, John, Romans and other books to crowds in Antioch and Constantinople. His recurring themes are repentance, care for the poor, the dangers of wealth and theatre, and the coming judgment, often pressed with vivid warnings about hell as a spur to moral reform. He also celebrates Christ's victory over death; the widely used Paschal Homily is traditionally attributed to him.
17724: Augustine: grace, the two cities and eternal punishment
17727: Augustine's preaching and writing stress humanity's bondage in original sin, the priority of God's grace, and the pilgrim City of God living among the earthly city. In *City of God* he reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church, and defends eternal punishment against those who hoped for a merciful end to hell. His handbook on catechising beginners tells the gospel as the whole biblical story from creation to the church.
17728: Western theology turns decisively toward questions of sin, grace and individual destiny. Augustine's non-literal reading of the millennium sidelines earthly-kingdom hopes for centuries, and his tentative openness to purifying fire after death becomes one root of purgatory. Eastern churches received his influence much less.
17735: Emperor Justinian issued an edict against Origen's teachings (543), and fifteen anathemas against Origenist doctrines, including pre-existence of souls and a restoration of all things, are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553).
17736: The scope is debated. Many scholars, following the acts as edited and translated by Richard Price, think the fifteen anathemas were approved by bishops before the council formally opened and are not in its official acts; canon 11 of the council does name Origen among heretics, though some argue that name is an interpolation. Others hold that the council effectively ratified the condemnation. Either way, universal restoration became a marginal position in both East and West, and eternal punishment became the settled public teaching.
17737: Gregory the Great: preaching the end and purgatorial fire
17738: Pope Gregory, convinced that the world was near its end amid plague and war, preached urgent repentance and pastoral care. His *Dialogues* include stories of souls purged after death and affirm a purifying fire for lesser faults before judgment, along with the help offered by masses for the dead. He also sent missionaries to the English (597).
17740: Irish penitentials and private, repeatable penance
17741: Ireland and Irish missions on the Continent
17744: Irish monks spread a form of penance that was private, repeatable and governed by handbooks (penitentials) assigning specific penances to specific sins. Confession to a priest and performing the assigned satisfaction became the ordinary path for Christians to deal with sin after baptism.
17745: The once-only public penance of the early church gives way to regular private confession. Pastoral attention increasingly centres on cataloguing sins and their remedies, a shift later formalised at Lateran IV.
17750: Anselm argues that sin is failing to render God the honour due to him, that justice requires satisfaction which humanity owes but cannot pay, and that only one who is both God and human can pay it. Christ freely offers his life, which outweighs all sin, and its merit flows to those he saves.
17751: The atonement explanation moves from victory over the devil and the restoration of creation toward satisfaction of God's honour or justice. Abelard soon stressed Christ's love awakening ours, Aquinas integrated multiple models, and the Reformers later reworked satisfaction into penal substitution. Scholars disagree on how novel Anselm was and whether feudal honour language shaped him decisively.
17755: The council required every Christian who had reached the age of discretion to confess all sins to their own priest at least once a year and to receive communion at least at Easter (canon 21). It also defined the eucharistic change as transubstantiation (canon 1).
17756: Sacramental penance becomes a universal, regulated duty. Preaching manuals and confessors' handbooks multiply, and the moral examination of individual sins becomes central to lay piety. Together with the developing doctrine of purgatory, this shapes the late-medieval economy of penance and indulgences.
17758: The friars and popular penitential preaching
17759: Assisi, Bologna and the towns of Europe
17764: Franciscans and Dominicans took preaching into towns, calling crowds to penance, confession and imitation of Christ's poverty and passion. Late-medieval preachers, art (Last Judgment portals, Dooms) and hymns such as *Dies irae* made death, judgment, heaven, hell and purgatory vivid. Some, such as Vincent Ferrer, preached that the end was imminent.
17770: In the short-lived union decree with the Greeks (*Laetentur caeli*), the council taught that the truly penitent who die before making full satisfaction are purified after death and helped by the suffrages of the living, while those in mortal sin go immediately to hell and the purified to heaven. A later decree (*Cantate Domino*, 1442) stated strongly that those outside the Catholic Church cannot be saved.
17771: Purgatory and the destiny of the individual soul at death are now conciliar teaching (building on Lyon II, 1274, and *Benedictus Deus*, 1336). The Greeks largely rejected the union, and their objections to a fire of purgatory persisted. This framework of satisfaction, purgatory and indulgences is what Luther attacked.
17772: Luther: the gospel as promise of forgiveness
17774: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses begin by saying that Christ willed the whole life of believers to be repentance, and argue that the church's true treasure is the gospel of God's glory and grace. In the 1520 treatises he presents the gospel as God's promise of forgiveness received by faith alone, freeing the conscience from the penitential system. His Small Catechism nevertheless frames redemption as being purchased to belong to Christ and live under him in his kingdom.
17775: Justification by faith becomes the hinge of preaching; the law-gospel pattern (terrify the conscience with the law, comfort it with the promise) shapes Protestant homiletics. Purgatory, indulgences and the sacrifice of the mass are rejected. Critics, then and now, ask whether the kingdom and new-creation horizons narrowed into individual justification; defenders say Luther's theology of the cross and two kingdoms keep a wider scope.
17779: Anabaptists: discipleship and the kingdom community
17784: Radical reformers preached faith that issues in costly following of Christ, believers' baptism, a disciplined community separate from the sword, and non-resistance. The Schleitheim Confession set out these articles. Faith was understood as yielding to Christ's lordship in ordinary life, not only trust in forgiveness.
17785: A minority strand insists that the gospel creates a visible kingdom people now. Persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike, it later influences Mennonite, Baptist and modern kingdom-ethics movements. Some early radicals (Münster, 1534–35) took apocalyptic expectation into violence, which most Anabaptists repudiated.
17787: Calvin and the Reformed: justification and union with Christ
17790: Calvin calls justification the main hinge of religion but places it within union with Christ, which also yields sanctification. He presents Christ in the threefold office of prophet, priest and king and gives sustained attention to the final resurrection. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) frames the faith as guilt, grace and gratitude, opening with the comfort of belonging to Christ in life and death.
17793: Council of Trent: justification and penance reaffirmed
17797: Trent's decree on justification taught that justification begins with God's prevenient grace, that faith is the beginning of salvation, and that justification is both forgiveness and inner renewal, with grace increasing through good works. It reaffirmed sacramental penance, purgatory and the veneration of saints while ordering reform of indulgence abuses and of preaching.
17798: Catholic and Protestant gospels harden into rival confessions. Catholic reform produces renewed preaching orders and missions (Jesuits), while Protestants read Trent as rejecting faith alone. The 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Lutheran–Catholic) claimed a consensus on basic truths; its significance is itself debated.
17800: John Wesley: assurance, new birth and holiness
17803: Wesley described his heart being strangely warmed at Aldersgate in May 1738 as he received assurance that his sins were forgiven. Taking up field preaching in 1739, he proclaimed salvation by faith, the new birth, the witness of the Spirit and the call to holiness of heart and life (Christian perfection), and organised converts into societies, classes and bands.
17804: The felt experience of conversion and assurance becomes a test of genuine faith, and holiness becomes a central aim of evangelistic preaching. Arminian Methodism and Calvinist revivalists disagree sharply about election while sharing this new experiential focus.
